Transactional enqueueing
========================

Transactional enqueueing is a key benefit of River. This model avoids several common failure modes of background jobs in a distributed application. It reduces the time spent investigating or engineering around distributed systems edge cases, and results in a simpler architecture.

* * *

Failures with two primary stores[](#failures-with-two-primary-stores)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

The alternative to River’s approach of putting a job queue in your main database is the traditional model of having two data stores — a primary database and a secondary store like Redis where jobs are enqueued. While largely functional, the two store approach can lead to data loss on the edges that’s nearly impossible to fully reconcile.

### Enqueue after transaction[](#enqueue-after-transaction)

Imagine building a user signup flow. The frontend submits an email and password to the backend application’s `POST /users` route. This request opens a database transaction to insert the user record into Postgres, which completes successfully. Then the backend application attempts to enqueue a job in Redis to send a welcome email to the user. ⚡ _**Zap!—the server just lost power.**_ ⚡  That user will never receive a signup confirmation email.

This chain of events might sound familiar to any seasoned backend developer. If it’s not a power loss, it could be a program panic, a network interruption, or any number of other failure modes that are possible when coordinating between two independent data stores (Postgres and Redis).

While such events may sound unlikely, in practice they turn out to be a regular frustration, especially at nontrivial scale.

### Enqueue before transaction completes?[](#enqueue-before-transaction-completes)

In previous example, the developer tried to enqueue the job _after_ the primary database transaction completed. This ensured that the database changes were committed _atomically_ (all at once or none at all), but it left open the possibility of the subsequent jobs being enqueued. What if the developer tried the opposite approach, and enqueued the job in Redis before the Postgres transaction commits?

The Redis worker picks up the new job in only a couple of milliseconds. As the worker queries the database to load the user record from the database by its ID, they hit an error — it seems the user does not exist in the database yet.

The diligent developer notices an error in their exception tracker and immediately digs in. They are puzzled to see that the `POST /users` request was successful, yet somehow their worker could not find the user record in the database. How could that be?

The answer is that the job was fetched from the Redis queue _before_ the Postgres database transaction committed the new user record, and thanks to rules around transaction visibility, the worker could not yet see that row when it queried for it. Or maybe the API encountered a subsequent error which caused the transaction to rollback and the user record was never actually committed. Or maybe the server encountered another power failure before it could commit.

A simpler model[](#a-simpler-model)
-----------------------------------

Transactional enqueueing solves all of the above problems, and it does so without needing to operate an additional service outside the primary Postgres database. When you enqueue a job in River, you can do so in a transaction with any other changes you’re making such as inserting a user record or adding a corresponding profile record. This means that when a worker picks up a job, it can rely on the fact that any data it depends on was already committed along with the job itself.

When you build your system around transactional enqueueing, you spend less time tracking down and patching around distributed systems edge cases and more time focusing on building what matters. In the past this model was held back by poor implementations or Postgres limitations, but this is no longer the case: a modern Postgres job queue can easily scale to tens of thousands of jobs per second.

We believe this should be the default model for building reliable systems, appropriate for all but the very largest applications.

Snoozing jobs
=============

Snoozing allows a worker to try a job again at a later time without counting the attempt as a failure. The job will be put back into the queue and scheduled to run again after the specified duration.

* * *

Snoozing a job[](#snoozing-a-job)
---------------------------------

Under normal circumstances, jobs that return an error are scheduled [to be retried](/docs/job-retries). This is done under the assumption that the problem they ran into was intermittent, or can be corrected by a code deploy that fixes a worker bug. However, sometimes a worker might want to execute the same job again in the future, even if no error has occurred.

While this could be achieved by enqueueing a new job, doing so can result in having many separate jobs in the database. The other option is to return an error from the job, but that doesn’t offer control over the retry interval and can eventually cause the job to exhaust its maximum attempts. Snoozing avoids these issues.

*   [Go](#tab-panel-0-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-0-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-0-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-0-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-0-4)

To snooze a job for later execution, return the result of [`JobSnooze`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#JobSnooze) from a worker:

    func (w *SnoozingWorker) Work(ctx context.Context, j *river.Job[SnoozingArgs]) error {    if tryAgainLater {        return river.JobSnooze(30*time.Second)    }    return nil}

See the [`JobSnooze` example](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#example-package-JobSnooze) for complete code.

`JobSnooze` takes one argument — the duration (after `time.Now()`) to snooze until the job should be attempted again. It returns an error that River will recognize as a signal to snooze the job (rather than counting it as an actual error).

Call `context.snooze` to end this attempt and try again later without consuming a retry:

    import java.time.Duration;
    builder.worker(snoozingJob, context -> {    if (tryAgainLater(context.job())) {        context.snooze(Duration.ofSeconds(30));    }});

Snoozing throws a control exception; let it propagate to River.

Raise `River.job_snooze` with a duration in seconds:

    def work(job)  raise River.job_snooze(30) if try_again_later?end

Return a snooze outcome:

    use std::time::Duration;use riverqueue::{BoxError, Job, WorkContext, WorkOutcome};
    async fn work(_context: WorkContext, _job: Job<SnoozingArgs>) -> Result<WorkOutcome, BoxError> {    if try_again_later() {        return Ok(WorkOutcome::Snooze(Duration::from_secs(30)));    }    Ok(WorkOutcome::Complete)}

Return `snooze` from the handler when the job should try again later. This example requests a thirty-second delay:

    import { snooze } from "riverqueue";
    workers.add(snoozingJob, async ({ job }) => {  if (await tryAgainLater(job)) return snooze({ seconds: 30 });});

The job becomes eligible to run again after the snooze duration. Short snoozes can be fetched directly when due; longer snoozes pass through the [scheduler](/docs/maintenance-services#scheduler). Polling, maintenance intervals, and worker capacity can add a delay.

No impact on retries[](#no-impact-on-retries)
---------------------------------------------

Snoozing is an intentional decision by the worker to try a job again later and isn’t considered an error. By extension, snoozing does not affect a job’s [retry](/docs/job-retries) behavior. Each time a job is snoozed, its attempt count is decremented by one so that a job can keep snoozing indefinitely without exhausting its maximum attempts. If a snoozed job later encounters an error and requires a retry, the previous snoozes will not be counted as errors when determining the retry backoff duration.

Metadata[](#metadata)
---------------------

When a job is snoozed, a counter is incremented in the `"snoozes"` metadata field:

    { "snoozes": 1 }

Unique jobs
===========

Jobs can be made unique, such that River guarantees that only one exists for a given set of properties. Jobs can be made unique by args, kind, period, queue, and state.

* * *

Unique properties[](#unique-properties)
---------------------------------------

It’s occasionally useful to ensure that background work is only performed once for a given set of conditions. For example, there might be a job that does a daily reconciliation of a user’s account, but performs heavy lifting across many accounts, so ideally it only runs once a day per account to save on worker resources. River can guarantee job uniqueness along dimensions based on a combination of job properties like arguments and insert period.

*   [Go](#tab-panel-0-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-0-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-0-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-0-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-0-4)

Jobs configure unique properties by implementing [`JobArgsWithInsertOpts`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#JobArgsWithInsertOpts) and populating [`UniqueOpts`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#UniqueOpts) as part of the [`InsertOpts`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#InsertOpts) returned, or by adding `UniqueOpts` at insertion time with [`Client.Insert`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#Client.Insert), `InsertTx`, or any of the `InsertMany*` bulk insertion methods.

    type ReconcileAccountArgs struct {    AccountID int `json:"account_id"`}
    func (ReconcileAccountArgs) Kind() string { return "reconcile_account" }
    // InsertOpts returns custom insert options that every job of this type will// inherit, including unique options.func (ReconcileAccountArgs) InsertOpts() river.InsertOpts {    return river.InsertOpts{        UniqueOpts: river.UniqueOpts{            ByArgs:   true,            ByPeriod: 24 * time.Hour,        },    }}
    ...
    // First job insertion for account 1._, err = riverClient.Insert(ctx, ReconcileAccountArgs{AccountID: 1}, nil)if err != nil {    panic(err)}
    // Job is inserted a second time, but it doesn't matter because its unique// args cause the insertion to be skipped because it's meant to only run// once per account per 24 hour period._, err = riverClient.Insert(ctx, ReconcileAccountArgs{AccountID: 1}, nil)if err != nil {    panic(err)}
    // Because the job is unique ByArgs, another job for account 2 _is_ allowed._, err = riverClient.Insert(ctx, ReconcileAccountArgs{AccountID: 2}, nil)if err != nil {    panic(err)}

See the [`UniqueJob` example](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#example-package-UniqueJob) for complete code.

Set uniqueness options on the job type. Matching arguments within the same twenty-four-hour period identify a duplicate:

    import com.riverqueue.Unique;import java.time.Duration;
    record ReconcileAccountArgs(long accountId) {}
    var reconcileAccount = JobType.of("reconcile_account", ReconcileAccountArgs.class)    .withDefaults(InsertOptions.builder()        .unique(Unique.args().per(Duration.ofHours(24)))        .build());
    client.insert(reconcileAccount, new ReconcileAccountArgs(1));
    // Returns the existing job during the same period.client.insert(reconcileAccount, new ReconcileAccountArgs(1));
    // Different arguments allow another job.client.insert(reconcileAccount, new ReconcileAccountArgs(2));

Pass `UniqueOpts` at insertion time to combine uniqueness by arguments and time period. The repeated insertion for account 1 returns the existing job:

    opts = River::UniqueOpts.new(by_args: true, by_period: 24 * 3600)client.insert ReconcileAccountArgs.new(account_id: 1), unique_opts: opts
    # Returns the existing job during the same period.client.insert ReconcileAccountArgs.new(account_id: 1), unique_opts: opts
    # Different arguments allow another job.client.insert ReconcileAccountArgs.new(account_id: 2), unique_opts: opts

Declare uniqueness on the args type with `unique(...)`. Combining `by_args` and `by_period` gives each account its own job within the period:

    #[derive(Clone, Debug, serde::Deserialize, riverqueue::JobArgs, serde::Serialize)]#[river(kind = "reconcile_account", unique(by_args, by_period = "24h"))]struct ReconcileAccountArgs {    account_id: i64,}
    client.insert(ReconcileAccountArgs { account_id: 1 }).await?;
    // Returns the existing job during the same period.client.insert(ReconcileAccountArgs { account_id: 1 }).await?;
    // Different arguments allow another job.client.insert(ReconcileAccountArgs { account_id: 2 }).await?;

Put uniqueness options in the job definition’s defaults. Here, matching arguments within the same twenty-four-hour period identify a duplicate:

    const reconcileAccount = defineJob({  kind: "reconcile_account",  schema: z.object({ account_id: z.number().int() }),  defaults: { unique: { byArgs: true, byPeriod: { hours: 24 } } },});
    await client.insert(reconcileAccount, { account_id: 1 });
    // Returns the existing job during the same period.await client.insert(reconcileAccount, { account_id: 1 });
    // Different arguments allow another job.await client.insert(reconcileAccount, { account_id: 2 });

Each unique dimension increases the specificity of the key, allowing more distinct jobs. Kind is included unless explicitly excluded. With a daily period alone, one job of that kind is allowed per period. Adding arguments allows one per set of encoded arguments per period. With no unique options, no uniqueness is enforced.

### Unique by args[](#unique-by-args)

Uniqueness by arguments compares the encoded JSON. `{"account_id":1}` can coexist with `{"account_id":2}`, but a second job with `{"account_id":1}` conflicts.

Top-level keys are sorted before hashing; nested keys are not sorted recursively. When inserting from different languages, agree on JSON field names, values, number representations, and nested key ordering so equivalent jobs produce the same unique key.

#### Using a subset of args[](#using-a-subset-of-args)

*   [Go](#tab-panel-1-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-1-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-1-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-1-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-1-4)

Sometimes it’s desirable to only use a subset of the args for uniqueness. For example you may want only one of a particular kind of job to exist for a given customer, but the args also contain something random like a trace ID. To opt into this mode, the fields considered for uniqueness can be flagged with a struct tag:

    type ReconcileAccountArgs struct {    CustomerID int    `json:"customer_id" river:"unique"`    TraceID    string `json:"trace_id"`}

Select fields on the job type with `uniqueBy` and enable argument uniqueness in insertion options. Use serialized JSON names, which are snake\_case by default:

    record CustomerArgs(long customerId, String message) {}
    var reconcileCustomer = JobType.of("reconcile_customer", CustomerArgs.class)    .uniqueBy("customer_id");
    client.insert(reconcileCustomer, new CustomerArgs(42, "reconcile"),    InsertOptions.builder().unique(Unique.args()).build());

Select the fields in `by_args`; unselected fields do not affect uniqueness:

    client.insert args, unique_opts: River::UniqueOpts.new(by_args: [:customer_id])

Mark the fields that participate in uniqueness with `#[river(unique)]`. In this example, `trace_id` can vary without creating a distinct job:

    #[derive(Clone, Debug, serde::Deserialize, riverqueue::JobArgs, serde::Serialize)]#[river(kind = "reconcile_account", unique(by_args))]struct ReconcileAccountArgs {    #[river(unique)]    customer_id: i64,    trace_id: String,}

Pass an array of argument names as `byArgs` to compare only those fields for uniqueness:

    await client.insert(reconcileAccount, args, {  unique: { byArgs: ["customer_id"] },});

### Unique by period[](#unique-by-period)

Uniqueness by period compares the job kind and a time interval. On insertion, the current time is rounded down to the nearest multiple of the given period, and a job is only inserted if there isn’t already an existing job that has been created at or scheduled to run between this lower bound and the next multiple of the period.

For example, if a job is inserted with a fifteen-minute unique period and the current time is 15:21:00, it’ll be unique for the interval of 15:15:00 to 15:30:00. A new job inserted at 15:28:00 will be skipped on grounds of uniqueness, but one inserted at 15:31:00 would be allowed.

The period is the most commonly used unique property, and other properties are most likely to be specified along with it, rather than be configured by themselves.

### Unique by queue[](#unique-by-queue)

Uniqueness by queue includes the queue name in the unique key.

For example, if a job with kind `reconcile_account` is inserted into queue `default`, a new insertion of `reconcile_account` would be skipped on grounds of uniqueness, but a `reconcile_account` inserted to queue `high_priority` would be allowed.

### Unique by state[](#unique-by-state)

Uniqueness by state controls which job states prevent another insertion. The default includes `available`, `completed`, `pending`, `running`, `retryable`, and `scheduled`; it excludes `cancelled` and `discarded`.

This default is usually the right setting for most unique jobs, but a custom value might be useful in tweaking behavior. For example, removing `completed` from the set above would mean that uniqueness would be enforced within active job states (i.e. being run or available to be run), so that each time a job with this kind completes, a new one is allowed to be enqueued.

Required states

When customizing the unique state list list, some states are required because River doesn’t have conflict resolution for all required internal transitions. The `pending`, `scheduled`, `available`, and `running` states are required whenever customizing this list.

If `retryable` is removed from the list, it’s possible for an erroring job to hit a conflict when it is retried (because a duplicate has since been inserted). In this scenario, River will move the conflicting job to `discarded` since it cannot be retried.

#### Job retention horizons[](#job-retention-horizons)

When thinking about job state, remember that completed jobs [aren’t retained permanently](/docs/maintenance-services#cleaner). The default retention time for completed jobs is 24 hours, so with a default unique state list, even with no unique period set a new job would be allowed to be inserted every 24 hours as the previous completed job is pruned.

-------------------------------------------------------------

Insert functions return [`JobInsertResult`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river/rivertype#JobInsertResult), containing a `UniqueSkippedAsDuplicate` property that’s set to true if an insert was skipped due to uniqueness:

    insertRes, err := riverClient.Insert(ctx, SortArgs{...}, nil)insertRes.UniqueSkippedAsDuplicate // true if job was skipped

`JobInsertResult.Job` contains a newly inserted job row, or the preexisting one with matching unique conditions if insertion was skipped.

Check `uniqueSkippedAsDuplicate` on the result. `job` is the inserted or existing row:

    var result = client.insert(reconcileAccount, new ReconcileAccountArgs(1));
    System.out.println(result.uniqueSkippedAsDuplicate());System.out.println(result.job().id());

Check `unique_skipped_as_duplicate?` on the insertion result to distinguish a new job from a matching existing one:

    result = client.insert args, unique_opts: opts
    result.unique_skipped_as_duplicate? # true if an existing job matchedresult.job # the inserted or existing job

Inspect `unique_skipped_as_duplicate` on the insertion result to see whether uniqueness prevented a new row:

    let result = client.insert(args).await?;
    println!("Duplicate: {}", result.unique_skipped_as_duplicate);println!("Job ID: {}", result.id());

Check for a `"duplicate"` status on the insertion result. Its `job` contains the existing row when uniqueness skips the insert:

    const result = await client.insert(reconcileAccount, args);
    console.log(result.status === "duplicate");console.log(result.job.id); // The inserted or existing job.

At least once[](#at-least-once)
-------------------------------

While River can ensure that a unique job is only inserted once, it can’t guarantee that it will be worked exactly once. A unique job could work successfully, but fail to have its completed status persisted to the database, which would require that it be worked again for River to be sure it went through. Like other jobs, River provides an at-least-once guarantee for unique jobs.

Unique jobs execute at least once

Although unique jobs ensure that a given job will only be _inserted_ once for the chosen properties, those jobs can still execute more than once due to River’s at-least-once execution design.

See [Reliable workers](/docs/reliable-workers) for more information.

Unique index[](#unique-index)
-----------------------------

Job uniqueness is enforced with a special partial unique index on the `river_job` table. The unique index only applies to jobs whose state is within its specified list of unique states, which can be customized on a per-job basis.

Maintenance services
====================

River includes a number of auxiliary services for features and queue maintenance. These perform functions like cleaning cancelled, completed, and discarded jobs from the database, periodically rebuilding indexes to optimize performance, and rescuing stuck jobs. One client at a time runs maintenance services, determined by [leader election](/docs/leader-election).

* * *

Cleaner[](#cleaner)
-------------------

River leaves cancelled, completed, and discarded jobs in the database even though they’re at the end of their lifecycle so that operators can introspect them, but if left to accumulate forever, they’d eventually grow the jobs table to a point where its size would consume excessive storage and impact performance.

To prevent the jobs table growing without bound, River includes a job cleaner process that periodically prunes old jobs. It wakes up periodically and deletes completed, cancelled, and permanently failed (discarded) jobs if their last attempt was beyond the retention period.

*   [Go](#tab-panel-0-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-0-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-0-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-0-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-0-4)

The default retention periods vary by job state, and each is configurable in [`Config`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#Config):

*   Cancelled: `CancelledJobRetentionPeriod`, defaults to 24 hours.
*   Completed: `CompletedJobRetentionPeriod`, defaults to 24 hours.
*   Discarded: `DiscardedJobRetentionPeriod`, defaults to 7 days.

Set retention for cancelled, completed, and discarded jobs, in that order:

    import java.time.Duration;
    builder.retention(Duration.ofDays(1), Duration.ofDays(1), Duration.ofDays(7));

A negative duration retains jobs in that state indefinitely.

Set retention periods in seconds on `River::Config`. This configuration keeps cancelled and completed jobs for a day and discarded jobs for a week:

    config = River::Config.new(  cancelled_job_retention_period: 86_400,  completed_job_retention_period: 86_400,  discarded_job_retention_period: 7 * 86_400)

Durations are seconds; `nil` or `-1` retains a state indefinitely.

Configure a `Retention` policy for each final job state and pass the resulting maintenance configuration to the client builder:

    use riverqueue::{MaintenanceConfig, Retention};use std::time::Duration;
    let maintenance = MaintenanceConfig::default()    .with_cancelled_job_retention(Retention::DeleteAfter(Duration::from_secs(86_400)))    .with_completed_job_retention(Retention::DeleteAfter(Duration::from_secs(86_400)))    .with_discarded_job_retention(Retention::DeleteAfter(Duration::from_secs(7 * 86_400)));
    let client = riverqueue::Client::builder(pool).maintenance(maintenance).build()?;

Use `Retention::Keep` to retain a state indefinitely.

Set retention durations under `maintenance` to control how long jobs remain in each final state:

    const client = new Client(driver, {  maintenance: {    cancelledJobRetention: { hours: 24 },    completedJobRetention: { hours: 24 },    discardedJobRetention: { hours: 168 },  },});

Use `null` to retain a state indefinitely.

### Workflow-aware retention[](#workflow-aware-retention)

River Pro workflows have auxiliary data in addition to their task jobs, including workflow rows, attempts, signals, timers, and evaluator worklist rows. By default, workflow task jobs still use the normal per-job retention behavior described above, including [per-queue retention](/docs/pro/per-queue-job-retention) and [dead letter queue](/docs/pro/dead-letter-queue) movement for discarded jobs. After all jobs and dead letter rows for a finalized workflow are gone, the Pro cleaner removes the remaining workflow metadata.

*   [Go](#tab-panel-1-0)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-1-1)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-1-2)

For installations that want workflow history to remain together, enable [`riverpro.Config.WorkflowAwareRetention`](/pkg/riverpro/latest/riverpro#Config). With workflow-aware retention enabled, workflow task jobs are excluded from normal per-job cleanup, and discarded workflow tasks are not moved to the dead letter queue before the workflow is cleaned. Finalized workflows are deleted as a unit:

*   `closed` workflows use `WorkflowClosedRetentionPeriod`, which defaults to 24 hours.
*   `cancelled` workflows use `WorkflowCancelledRetentionPeriod`, which defaults to 24 hours.

    riverClient, err := riverpro.NewClient(riverpropgxv5.New(dbPool), &riverpro.Config{    Config: river.Config{        Queues: map[string]river.QueueConfig{            river.QueueDefault: {MaxWorkers: 100},        },        Workers: workers,    },    WorkflowAwareRetention:          true,    WorkflowClosedRetentionPeriod:   30 * 24 * time.Hour,    WorkflowCancelledRetentionPeriod: 7 * 24 * time.Hour,})if err != nil {    return err}

Set either workflow retention period to `-1` to preserve workflows in that state indefinitely. Setting both periods to `-1` keeps finalized workflow data indefinitely, including task jobs, dead letter jobs, attempts, timers, signals, and wait-condition evidence.

Enable `workflow_aware_retention` on `River::Pro::Config` to keep finalized workflows together. Retention periods are in seconds and default to 24 hours for both states:

    client = River::Pro::Client.new(driver,  config: River::Pro::Config.new(    core: River::Config.new(queues: {default: 100}, workers: workers),    workflow_aware_retention: true,    workflow_closed_retention_period: 30 * 24 * 3600,    workflow_cancelled_retention_period: 7 * 24 * 3600  ))

Set either period to `nil` or `-1` to retain workflows in that state indefinitely. Workflow tasks are excluded from ordinary per-job cleanup and dead letter movement; jobs, signals, timers, and attempt history are cleaned together.

Enable workflow-aware cleanup on the Pro builder with `WorkflowRetention`:

    use riverqueue::{QueueConfig, Retention, database::PostgresDatabase};use riverqueue_pro::{ProClient, WorkflowRetention};use std::time::Duration;
    let client = ProClient::builder(PostgresDatabase::new(pool))    .queue("default", QueueConfig::new(100))    .workers(workers)    .workflow_aware_retention(        WorkflowRetention::default()            .with_closed_retention(Retention::DeleteAfter(Duration::from_secs(                30 * 24 * 60 * 60,            )))            .with_cancelled_retention(Retention::DeleteAfter(Duration::from_secs(                7 * 24 * 60 * 60,            ))),    )    .build()?;

Both periods default to 24 hours; set either to `Retention::Keep` to retain workflows in that state indefinitely. Workflow tasks are excluded from ordinary job cleanup and dead letter movement. Finalized workflows, their jobs, signals, timers, and attempt history are cleaned together.

Workflow-aware retention changes cleanup semantics

When workflow-aware retention is enabled, workflow task jobs no longer follow their individual finalized timestamps, per-queue retention periods, or dead letter movement. Use it when workflow-level auditability is more important than cleaning each task according to normal job retention.

Periodic enqueuer[](#periodic-enqueuer)
---------------------------------------

The periodic enqueuer schedules [periodic jobs](/docs/periodic-jobs). On start, it calculates the next run time of every configured periodic job, then runs in a loop:

*   Sleeps until the next run time of the first job that’ll come due.
*   Runs the job and any others that’ll come due within a small margin of now.
*   Recalculates the next run time of all jobs that ran.
*   Goes back to sleep and repeats the cycle.

The periodic enqueuer has no configuration aside from its assigned periodic jobs.

* * *

Queue cleaner[](#queue-cleaner)
-------------------------------

The `river_queue` table is used to track active queues and powers features such as [pause and resume](/docs/pausing-queues). To avoid this table remaining bloated with queues that are no longer in use, a queue cleaner maintenance process is responsible for periodically deleting the records of any queues which have not been used within the past 24 hours (based on their `updated_at` timestamp).

Queue-cleaner configuration varies by language. Rust and TypeScript expose intervals and retention through their maintenance configuration; Go, Java, and Ruby use the built-in queue retention behavior.

Reindexer[](#reindexer)
-----------------------

The reindexer works periodically to issue a [`REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-reindex.html) to rebuild certain key job indexes. In most situations reindexing isn’t expected to improve performance, but it can help in some degenerate cases like where a glut of jobs had at one point bloated the B-tree index and subsequently left it with many empty or nearly empty pages. In such situations Postgres’ indexes will never “collapse” of their own accord, but a `REINDEX` to rebuild them from scratch produces a new index with the live rows and without the empty space.

The reindexer rebuilds one index at a time in order to not put an undue amount of stress on the database.

*   [Go](#tab-panel-2-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-2-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-2-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-2-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-2-4)

By default the reindexer runs every day at midnight UTC, but it can be customized through [`Config.ReindexerSchedule`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#Config) with a custom scheduling function. Like with periodic jobs, a [cron package](/docs/periodic-jobs#complex-cron-schedules) can be used to succinctly define a complex schedule. It can be disabled altogether using `river.NeverSchedule()` as its schedule.

By default the reindexer only rebuilds indexes in `river_job`, the table by far the most prone to index bloat. The default list of indexes is available in [`ReindexerIndexNamesDefault`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#ReindexerIndexNamesDefault) and can be customized with [`Config.ReindexerIndexNames`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#Config).

Configure the Postgres indexes to rebuild and the interval between runs:

    builder.reindex(List.of("river_job_args_index"), Duration.ofDays(1));

Pass an empty list to disable reindexing. Java does not expose a separate reindex timeout option.

Ruby does not currently run a built-in Postgres reindexer. If reindexing is needed, schedule it operationally or let an eligible Go, Rust, or TypeScript maintenance client perform it.

Configure Postgres reindexing on the database adapter:

    use riverqueue::database::{PostgresDatabase, PostgresReindexConfig};
    let database = PostgresDatabase::new(pool).with_reindex(    PostgresReindexConfig::default().with_timeout(std::time::Duration::from_secs(60)));
    let client = riverqueue::Client::builder(database).build()?;

The default schedule is midnight UTC. Use `with_schedule` to change it or an empty index-name list to disable rebuilding.

Set `reindexerTimeout` under `maintenance` to bound the time allowed for reindexing. This example allows one minute:

    const client = new Client(driver, {  maintenance: { reindexerTimeout: { minutes: 1 } },});

Use `maintenance.reindexerSchedule` to change the schedule, or an empty `reindexerIndexNames` list to disable rebuilding. This service applies only to Postgres.

### Reindex artifacts[](#reindex-artifacts)

`REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY` may leave behind partially built indexes if a reindex attempt doesn’t complete. Postgres names these artifacts by adding `_ccnew` or `_ccold` to the original index name, like `river_job_args_index_ccnew` or `river_job_args_index_ccold`. After multiple failed attempts, Postgres may add a numeric suffix like `river_job_args_index_ccnew1`.

When River finds one of these artifacts, it logs a warning and skips the reindex attempt instead of removing the artifact and trying again. The artifact usually means a previous reindex exceeded the configured reindex timeout, so another immediate attempt is likely to fail in the same way and put unnecessary pressure on the database.

To find all reindex artifacts attached to River’s `river_job` table:

    SELECT n.nspname AS schema_name,       c.relname AS index_nameFROM pg_class cJOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespaceJOIN pg_index i ON i.indexrelid = c.oidJOIN pg_class t ON t.oid = i.indrelidWHERE t.relname = 'river_job'  AND c.relname ~ '_cc(new|old)[0-9]*$'ORDER BY 1, 2;

You can get the reindexer running again by manually dropping indexes returned by the query above:

    DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS river_job_args_index_ccnew;DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS river_job_args_index_ccold;DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS river_job_metadata_index_ccnew;DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS river_job_metadata_index_ccold;

Make sure to qualify with a schema name when using [an alternate schema](/docs/alternate-schema).

If you had to remove reindexer artifacts, consider increasing the reindex timeout before re-enabling the reindexer or waiting for the next scheduled run, otherwise the next attempt may also fail and leave another artifact behind.

Rescuer[](#rescuer)
-------------------

In a mixed-language deployment, every client eligible for leadership needs to recognize the kinds it may rescue and use compatible timeout settings. Otherwise an unknown kind can be discarded by the leader. Disable leader election on clients that cannot provide that registry, and keep at least one fully configured maintenance client running.

The rescuer looks for “stuck” jobs and either enqueues them to be reworked, or discards them if they’ve hit their maximum allowed attempts. A job may become stuck in situations like:

*   A hardware crash causes the process to terminate before a job finished work or before it could be completed.
*   A worker blocks indefinitely or ignores cancellation. [Design jobs to be cancellable](/docs/graceful-shutdown#designing-cancellable-jobs) so normal shutdown can finalize interrupted attempts.
*   After the job ran, there was a problem persisting its new state to the database. This problem should be rare, and can be avoided completely with the use of [transactional job completion](/docs/transactional-job-completion).

*   [Go](#tab-panel-3-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-3-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-3-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-3-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-3-4)

The duration after which a job is considered stuck and eligible for rescue can be configured with [`Config.RescueStuckJobsAfter`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#Config). Its value:

*   Defaults to one hour, or `JobTimeout` plus one hour in case `JobTimeout` has been configured to be larger than one hour.
*   Must be greater than `JobTimeout` if both it and `JobTimeout` are configured.

Jobs that have overridden the default timeout by implementing `Timeout()` on their worker will be given at least that timeout duration before they’re considered stuck and eligible for rescue.

The rescuer bounds job duration

`Config.RescueStuckJobsAfter` is effectively an upper bound on how long jobs are allowed to run, because jobs that are still running after this duration will be rescheduled to run again, potentially alongside an existing execution attempt for the same job.

Set the age after which abandoned jobs can be rescued:

    builder.rescueAfter(Duration.ofHours(2));

The threshold must be at least as long as the runtime’s `jobTimeout`. It defaults to one hour plus an explicitly configured positive job timeout. The rescuer also evaluates [`Workers.Handler.timeout(job)`](/docs/reliable-workers#worker-level-job-timeouts) for each candidate, respecting longer worker deadlines and disabled timeouts. Register compatible handlers on every client eligible to lead.

Ruby checks stale running jobs after an hour and respects longer client or worker timeouts. A worker with its timeout disabled is not automatically rescued on the basis of age. There is no separate public rescue-age setting.

Set the rescue age through `MaintenanceConfig::with_rescue_after`. It must not be shorter than the client timeout. Worker-specific timeouts are also respected; disabling a worker timeout disables ordinary timeout-based rescue.

Configure `maintenance.rescueAfter`; the default is one hour. The rescuer respects worker-specific timeouts and skips ordinary timeout-based rescue when a timeout is disabled.

* * *

Scheduler[](#scheduler)
-----------------------

Jobs can be scheduled to run in the future for several reasons:

*   At insertion time, a future scheduled time was specified.
*   A worker may have [snoozed](/docs/snoozing-jobs) the job to run again in the future.
*   The job may have errored on a previous execution and needs to be [retried](/docs/job-retries) after a backoff duration.

The scheduler executes at a constant interval. Each time it runs, it queries for jobs that are ready to be attempted again and makes them `available`. Go’s scheduler runs every 5 seconds. Rust and TypeScript expose a scheduler interval in their maintenance configuration; Java and Ruby check due jobs as part of their maintenance loops.

Cancelling jobs
===============

Cancel a job when it should never run again, or request cancellation of an execution already in progress. A cancelled job is not retried automatically.

* * *

Cancelling from within a worker[](#cancelling-from-within-a-worker)
-------------------------------------------------------------------

Ordinary worker errors are [retried](/docs/job-retries), on the assumption that the problem is temporary or can be fixed by a code deploy. When a worker detects a permanent failure, such as an account that has been closed, it can cancel the job instead.

*   [Go](#tab-panel-0-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-0-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-0-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-0-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-0-4)

Return [`river.JobCancel`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#JobCancel) from the worker’s `Work` method:

    func (w *CancellingWorker) Work(ctx context.Context, j *river.Job[CancellingArgs]) error {    return river.JobCancel(fmt.Errorf("account has been closed"))}

The wrapped error is persisted in the job’s error history, so operators can see why it was cancelled. See the [`JobCancel` example](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#example-package-JobCancel) for complete code.

Call `context.cancel(reason)` to end the attempt and permanently cancel the job:

    record CancellingArgs() {}
    var cancelling = JobType.of("cancelling", CancellingArgs.class);var builder = Client.builder(database).worker(cancelling, context -> {    context.cancel("account has been closed");});

Cancellation exits the handler through a control exception. Let it propagate to River; throwing an ordinary exception follows the retry policy instead.

Raise the exception returned by `River.job_cancel` from the worker’s `work` method:

    class CancellingWorker  def self.kind = "cancelling"
      def work(job)    raise River.job_cancel("account has been closed")  endend

The message is persisted in the job’s error history. `River.job_cancel` also accepts an exception, preserving its message and retaining the original exception as its cause. Raise the result: returning the exception object alone does not cancel the job.

Return `Ok(WorkOutcome::Cancel)` from the worker’s `work` method. An ordinary `Err` follows the retry policy instead.

    use riverqueue::{Job, WorkContext, WorkOutcome, Worker};
    impl Worker<CancellingArgs> for CancellingWorker {    type Error = std::convert::Infallible;
        async fn work(        &self,        _context: WorkContext,        _job: Job<CancellingArgs>,    ) -> Result<WorkOutcome, Self::Error> {        Ok(WorkOutcome::Cancel)    }}

This records “job cancelled by worker” in the job’s error history. `WorkOutcome::Cancel` does not take a custom error message; log any additional context before returning it.

Return `cancel({ reason })` from the worker function registered with `Workers.add`:

    import { cancel, defineJob, Workers } from "riverqueue";
    const cancellingJob = defineJob({ kind: "cancelling" });
    const workers = new Workers().add(cancellingJob, async () => {  return cancel({ reason: "account has been closed" });});

The optional `reason` is persisted in the job’s error history as `JobCancelError: <reason>`. Return the outcome to cancel the job; throwing an ordinary error or rejecting the worker’s promise follows the retry policy instead.

Cancelling a job from the client[](#cancelling-a-job-from-the-client)
---------------------------------------------------------------------

Use a job’s ID to cancel it from a client, whether or not it is currently running. For an existing job, each method returns its current record; a running job may still be marked `running` while its worker responds to the request.

*   [Go](#tab-panel-1-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-1-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-1-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-1-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-1-4)

Call [`Client.JobCancel`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#Client.JobCancel):

    if _, err := riverClient.JobCancel(ctx, jobID); err != nil {    // handle error}

See the [`JobCancelFromClient` example](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#example-package-JobCancelFromClient) for complete code.

Call `Client.cancel` with the job’s `long` ID:

    var job = client.cancel(jobId);

A missing job throws `RiverException` with code `NOT_FOUND`. Pass an open JDBC transaction as the first argument to cancel transactionally.

Call `client.job_cancel(job_id)`:

    job = client.job_cancel(job_id)

This raises `River::NotFoundError` if the job does not exist. Database errors also propagate to the caller.

Call `client.jobs().cancel(job_id)` and await the request:

    let job = client.jobs().cancel(job_id).await?;

The request does not execute until it is awaited. Handle the returned error or propagate it with `?`.

Call `client.jobs.cancel(jobID)` and await the result. Job IDs are `bigint` values:

    const job = await client.jobs.cancel(jobID);

This returns `null` if the job does not exist. Database errors reject the promise; handle them with `try`/`catch` or let them propagate to the caller.

The result of cancellation depends on the job’s state and whether its worker finishes before the request takes effect. Cancellation does not undo work or external side effects that have already happened.

### Jobs still running[](#jobs-still-running)

Running jobs are marked for cancellation rather than immediately finalized. The client executing the job then signals or interrupts its worker. A worker can finish before this happens, and how it responds to the request depends on its language.

*   [Go](#tab-panel-2-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-2-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-2-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-2-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-2-4)

River cancels the worker’s `context.Context`. Go cannot interrupt a running goroutine, so the worker must respect context cancellation and return promptly. Pass `ctx` to database and HTTP calls, and check `ctx.Done()` in long-running loops or waits.

After a remote cancellation signal is received, returning an error cancels the job permanently. Returning `nil` still completes the job successfully.

If the worker finishes after the cancellation request is recorded but before it receives the signal:

*   If the job was due to be finalized because it completed successfully, was cancelled from within, or was discarded due to exceeding its max attempts, the job will be updated as usual.
*   If the job was snoozed to run again later or encountered a retryable error, the job will be marked as `cancelled` and will not be attempted again.

Cancellation is cooperative. Call `context.checkCancelled()` between units of work, use interruptible operations, and let `InterruptedException` propagate. River distinguishes remote cancellation from shutdown and timeouts.

`context.awaitCancellation()` waits for a cancellation request; it does not itself fail the attempt. Follow it with `context.checkCancelled()` when abandoning unfinished work. A handler that returns normally can still complete the job.

River checks running jobs for cancellation requests and raises `River::JobCancelError` in the worker thread when it finds one. Let this exception propagate to River. If you rescue `StandardError` inside a worker, re-raise `River::JobCancelError` instead of swallowing it or retrying the operation yourself.

Use `ensure` blocks or block-based resource management to release resources when work is interrupted. An uninterruptible native call can delay the worker’s response.

River also checks for cancellation before recording a successful completion, so a worker that returns normally can still be marked `cancelled` if the request is observed at that point. A job whose completion has already been recorded remains `completed`.

River signals `WorkContext::cancellation_token()`. Use the token’s `cancelled()` future with `tokio::select!` to stop long-running work and return promptly. The token is also used for timeouts and client shutdown, so a signalled token alone does not mean the job should be permanently cancelled. Return a `riverqueue::WorkCancelled` error to stop cooperatively and let River determine the outcome.

After a remote cancellation signal is received, returning an error cancels the job permanently. Returning `Ok(WorkOutcome::Complete)` still completes it successfully. A worker that ignores cancellation may eventually have its task aborted after the client’s stuck-job threshold.

If the worker finishes before it receives the signal, a recorded cancellation request prevents retry or snooze transitions from scheduling another attempt. A transition to a finalized state can still win the race.

River aborts the worker’s `signal`, an `AbortSignal`, with a `JobCancelledError`. Cancellation is cooperative: pass `signal` to operations that support it, such as `fetch`, and check `signal.throwIfAborted()` in long-running loops. Use `finally` for cleanup and let abort errors propagate to River.

After a remote cancellation signal is received, throwing or rejecting cancels the job permanently. Returning `snooze(...)` or `discard(...)` also cancels it. A worker that still resolves successfully, including by returning `complete()`, completes the job as usual.

The same signal is used for job timeouts and client shutdown. Let River distinguish those cases instead of converting every abort into a permanent `cancel()` outcome. An in-process worker that ignores its signal cannot be forcibly interrupted; the optional [`@riverqueue/worker-threads`](https://github.com/riverqueue/river/tree/master/js/worker-threads) runtime can terminate a worker thread after `jobStuckThreshold`.

If the worker finishes before receiving the signal, a recorded cancellation request prevents a retry or snooze from scheduling another attempt. A transition to a finalized state can still win the race.

### Jobs still enqueued[](#jobs-still-enqueued)

For jobs that have not started (`available`, `scheduled`, `retryable`, or `pending`), cancellation is straightforward. The job is immediately and atomically marked as `cancelled` so that no client will fetch it from the queue and it will not be attempted again. If a worker claims the job first, the running-job behavior above applies instead.

### Jobs already finalized[](#jobs-already-finalized)

If the job is already finalized (`cancelled`, `completed`, or `discarded`), no changes are made.

Job retries
===========

When River jobs encounter an error or other failure, they are automatically retried after a delay. The default retry policy backs off for `attempts ^ 4 + rand(±10%)` seconds (0s, 1s, 16s, …), and jobs will be tried a maximum of 25 times by default.

* * *

Limiting retry attempts[](#limiting-retry-attempts)
---------------------------------------------------

The default limit is 25 total attempts, including the initial run. Set it to one to disable retries for ordinary worker errors. Insertion options override defaults on the job kind.

*   [Go](#tab-panel-0-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-0-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-0-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-0-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-0-4)

River’s default is to retry jobs up to 25 times as defined by `river.DefaultMaxAttempts`. This can be customized for a given worker using the optional `JobArgsWithInsertOpts` interface on the `JobArgs` implementation:

    type RetryOnceJobArgs struct {}
    func (args RetryOnceJobArgs) Kind() string { return "RetryOnceJob" }
    func (args RetryOnceJobArgs) InsertOpts() river.InsertOpts {    return river.InsertOpts{MaxAttempts: 1}}

The max attempts can also be customized for an individual job at insertion time. This takes precedence over a job-level default:

    _, err = riverClient.Insert(ctx, RetryOnceJobArgs{}, &river.InsertOpts{    // use a max attempts of 5 for this one job even though the job has a    // default limit of 1:    MaxAttempts: 5,})

* * *

Set a default attempt limit on the job type, then override it for an individual insertion:

    var retryOnce = JobType.of("retry_once", RetryOnceArgs.class)    .withDefaults(InsertOptions.builder().maxAttempts(1).build());
    client.insert(retryOnce, new RetryOnceArgs(),    InsertOptions.builder().maxAttempts(5).build());

Set a default on argument objects or override it for one insertion:

    class RetryOnceJobArgs  def kind = "RetryOnceJob"  def to_json = JSON.generate({})  def insert_opts = River::InsertOpts.new(max_attempts: 1)end
    client.insert RetryOnceJobArgs.new, max_attempts: 5

Set `max_attempts` on the args type for the default limit, or override it on a particular insertion with `InsertOpts`:

    #[derive(Clone, Debug, serde::Deserialize, riverqueue::JobArgs, serde::Serialize)]#[river(kind = "RetryOnceJob", max_attempts = 1)]struct RetryOnceJobArgs {}
    client.insert(RetryOnceJobArgs {})    .opts(riverqueue::InsertOpts::default().with_max_attempts(5))    .await?;

Set `maxAttempts` in the job definition’s defaults, then override it in insertion options when an individual job needs a different limit:

    const retryOnce = defineJob({ kind: "RetryOnceJob", defaults: { maxAttempts: 1 } });await client.insert(retryOnce, {}, { maxAttempts: 5 });

Retry delays[](#retry-delays)
-----------------------------

Jobs are typically delayed for some amount of time between attempts. River provides reasonable default retry delays, but this behavior is also fully customizable at the client and worker level.

### Client retry policy[](#client-retry-policy)

The default retry policy uses a quartic backoff based on how many times the job has errored. A randomized ±10% jitter is applied to prevent stampeding errors from all retrying at the same time.

    attempts ^ 4 + rand(±10%)

A job which has errored repeatedly will see its retries delayed as shown below:

Attempt

Delay (±10%)

0 → 1

\-

Initial run before an error (no delay)

1 → 2

1s

Delay after first error

2 → 3

16s

3 → 4

1m21s

4 → 5

4m16s

5 → 6

10m25s

…

…

24 → 25

3d20h9m36s

Last retry, ~3 weeks after first run

The last retry comes about **three weeks** after the first time a job is worked, so in case of a buggy job, there’s plenty of time to get a fix out before the job is finally discarded.

*   [Go](#tab-panel-1-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-1-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-1-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-1-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-1-4)

The client retry policy can easily be customized:

    // LinearRetryPolicy delays subsequent retries by 5 seconds for each time// the job has failed (5s, 10s, 15s, etc.).type LinearRetryPolicy struct {}
    // NextRetry returns the next retry time based on the non-generic JobRow// which includes an up-to-date Errors list.func (policy *LinearRetryPolicy) NextRetry(job *rivertype.JobRow) time.Time {    // The latest error is not yet included in the job's Errors list, so we    // add 1 to the length to account for that.    return time.Now().Add(time.Duration(len(job.Errors) + 1) * 5 * time.Second)}
    client, err := river.NewClient(riverpgxv5.New(dbPool), &river.Config{    RetryPolicy: &LinearRetryPolicy{},    // ...})

Configure a retry policy on the client builder. It returns a delay, with the current failure not yet included in `job.errors()`:

    import java.time.Duration;
    builder.retryPolicy(job -> Duration.ofSeconds((job.errors().size() + 1) * 5L));

Provide a retry policy object whose `next_retry` method returns the next scheduled time. This example increases the delay by five seconds per recorded error:

    class LinearRetryPolicy  def next_retry(job, _error, now:)    now + (job.errors.length + 1) * 5  endend
    config = River::Config.new(retry_policy: LinearRetryPolicy.new)

Implement `RetryPolicy` to return the delay until the next attempt, then attach it to the client builder:

    struct LinearRetryPolicy;
    impl riverqueue::RetryPolicy for LinearRetryPolicy {    fn next_retry(        &self,        job: &riverqueue::JobRow,        _error: &riverqueue::WorkError,        _now: riverqueue::chrono::DateTime<riverqueue::chrono::Utc>,    ) -> std::time::Duration {        std::time::Duration::from_secs((job.errors.len() as u64 + 1) * 5)    }}
    let client = riverqueue::Client::builder(pool).retry_policy(LinearRetryPolicy).build()?;

Supply a `retryPolicy` callback that returns the next retry time. This example adds five seconds of delay for each recorded error:

    const client = new Client(driver, {  retryPolicy: (job, now) => now.add({ seconds: (job.errors.length + 1) * 5 }),});

### Customizing retry delays for a specific worker[](#customizing-retry-delays-for-a-specific-worker)

*   [Go](#tab-panel-2-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-2-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-2-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-2-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-2-4)

While the client retry policy applies to all kinds of jobs worked by that client, workers can also override the retry behavior for all jobs of that kind. This is done via the `Worker` interface’s `NextRetry(*Job[T]) time.Time` method. `WorkerDefaults` always returns 0 for this method to fallback to the client retry policy, so it can be customized for a given worker just by returning a non-zero value:

    type ConstantRetryTimeWorker struct {    river.WorkerDefaults[MyJobArgs]}
    func (w *ConstantRetryTimeWorker) Work(job *Job[MyJobArgs]) error {    // ...}
    // NextRetry always schedules the next retry for 10 seconds from now.func (w *ConstantRetryTimeWorker) NextRetry(job *Job[MyJobArgs]) time.Time {    return time.Now().Add(10*time.Second)}

Branch on the job kind in the runtime’s retry policy, falling back to River’s default for other kinds:

    import com.riverqueue.RetryPolicy;
    var defaultRetry = RetryPolicy.defaults();builder.retryPolicy(job -> job.kind().equals("my_job")    ? Duration.ofSeconds(10)    : defaultRetry.delay(job));

Define a worker’s `next_retry` method, returning an absolute time:

    def next_retry(_job, _error) = Time.now.utc + 10

Override `next_retry` in the worker’s `Worker` implementation. Return a delay, or `None` to use the client policy:

    fn next_retry(    &self,    _job: &riverqueue::Job<MyArgs>,    _error: &riverqueue::WorkError,    _now: riverqueue::chrono::DateTime<riverqueue::chrono::Utc>,) -> Option<std::time::Duration> {    Some(std::time::Duration::from_secs(10))}

Set `retryPolicy` when registering a handler to override the client’s policy for that worker. Here, each retry is scheduled ten seconds later:

    workers.add(myJob, handler, {  retryPolicy: (_job, now) => now.add({ seconds: 10 }),});

### Overview [¶](#pkg-overview "Go to Overview")

*   [Job args and workers](#hdr-Job_args_and_workers)
*   [Registering workers](#hdr-Registering_workers)
*   [Starting a client](#hdr-Starting_a_client)
*   [Inserting jobs](#hdr-Inserting_jobs)
*   [Other features](#hdr-Other_features)
*   [Development](#hdr-Development)

Package river is a robust high-performance job processing system for Go and Postgres.

See [homepage](https://riverqueue.com), [docs](https://riverqueue.com/docs), and [godoc](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river), as well as the [River UI](https://github.com/riverqueue/riverui).

Being built for Postgres, River encourages the use of the same database for application data and job queue. By enqueueing jobs transactionally along with other database changes, whole classes of distributed systems problems are avoided. Jobs are guaranteed to be enqueued if their transaction commits, are removed if their transaction rolls back, and aren't visible for work \_until\_ commit. See [transactional enqueueing](https://riverqueue.com/docs/transactional-enqueueing) for more background on this philosophy.

#### Job args and workers [¶](#hdr-Job_args_and_workers "Go to Job args and workers")

Jobs are defined in struct pairs, with an implementation of [\`JobArgs\`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#JobArgs) and one of [\`Worker\`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#Worker).

Job args contain \`json\` annotations and define how jobs are serialized to and from the database, along with a "kind", a stable string that uniquely identifies the job.

type SortArgs struct {
	// Strings is a slice of strings to sort.
	Strings \[\]string \`json:"strings"\`
}

func (SortArgs) Kind() string { return "sort" }

Workers expose a \`Work\` function that dictates how jobs run.

type SortWorker struct {
    // An embedded WorkerDefaults sets up default methods to fulfill the rest of
    // the Worker interface:
    river.WorkerDefaults\[SortArgs\]
}

func (w \*SortWorker) Work(ctx context.Context, job \*river.Job\[SortArgs\]) error {
    sort.Strings(job.Args.Strings)
    fmt.Printf("Sorted strings: %+v\\n", job.Args.Strings)
    return nil
}

#### Registering workers [¶](#hdr-Registering_workers "Go to Registering workers")

Jobs are uniquely identified by their "kind" string. Workers are registered on start up so that River knows how to assign jobs to workers:

workers := river.NewWorkers()
// AddWorker panics if the worker is already registered or invalid:
river.AddWorker(workers, &SortWorker{})

#### Starting a client [¶](#hdr-Starting_a_client "Go to Starting a client")

A River [\`Client\`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#Client) provides an interface for job insertion and manages job processing and [maintenance services](https://riverqueue.com/docs/maintenance-services). A client's created with a database pool, [driver](https://riverqueue.com/docs/database-drivers), and config struct containing a \`Workers\` bundle and other settings. Here's a client \`Client\` working one queue (\`"default"\`) with up to 100 worker goroutines at a time:

riverClient, err := river.NewClient(riverpgxv5.New(dbPool), &river.Config{
    Queues: map\[string\]river.QueueConfig{
        river.QueueDefault: {MaxWorkers: 100},
    },
    Workers: workers,
})
if err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

// Run the client inline. All executed jobs will inherit from ctx:
if err := riverClient.Start(ctx); err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

\## Insert-only clients

It's often desirable to have a client that'll be used for inserting jobs, but not working them. This is possible by omitting the \`Queues\` configuration, and skipping the call to \`Start\`:

riverClient, err := river.NewClient(riverpgxv5.New(dbPool), &river.Config{
    Workers: workers,
})
if err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

\`Workers\` can also be omitted, but it's better to include it so River can check that inserted job kinds have a worker that can run them.

\## Stopping

The client should also be stopped on program shutdown:

// Stop fetching new work and wait for active jobs to finish.
if err := riverClient.Stop(ctx); err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

There are some complexities around ensuring clients stop cleanly, but also in a timely manner. See [graceful shutdown](https://riverqueue.com/docs/graceful-shutdown) for more details on River's stop modes.

#### Inserting jobs [¶](#hdr-Inserting_jobs "Go to Inserting jobs")

[\`Client.InsertTx\`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#Client.InsertTx) is used in conjunction with an instance of job args to insert a job to work on a transaction:

\_, err = riverClient.InsertTx(ctx, tx, SortArgs{
    Strings: \[\]string{
        "whale", "tiger", "bear",
    },
}, nil)

if err != nil {
    panic(err)
}

See the [\`InsertAndWork\` example](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#example-package-InsertAndWork) for complete code.

#### Other features [¶](#hdr-Other_features "Go to Other features")

*   [Batch job insertion](https://riverqueue.com/docs/batch-job-insertion) for efficiently inserting many jobs at once using Postgres \`COPY FROM\`.
    
*   [Cancelling jobs](https://riverqueue.com/docs/cancelling-jobs) from inside a work function.
    
*   [Error and panic handling](https://riverqueue.com/docs/error-handling).
    
*   [Multiple queues](https://riverqueue.com/docs/multiple-queues) to better guarantee job throughput, worker availability, and isolation between components.
    
*   [Periodic and cron jobs](https://riverqueue.com/docs/periodic-jobs).
    
*   [Scheduled jobs](https://riverqueue.com/docs/scheduled-jobs) that run automatically at their scheduled time in the future.
    
*   [Snoozing jobs](https://riverqueue.com/docs/snoozing-jobs) from inside a work function.
    
*   [Subscriptions](https://riverqueue.com/docs/subscriptions) to queue activity and statistics, providing easy hooks for telemetry like logging and metrics.
    
*   [Test helpers](https://riverqueue.com/docs/testing) to verify that jobs are inserted as expected.
    
*   [Transactional job completion](https://riverqueue.com/docs/transactional-job-completion) to guarantee job completion commits with other changes in a transaction.
    
*   [Unique jobs](https://riverqueue.com/docs/unique-jobs) by args, period, queue, and state.
    
*   [Web UI](https://github.com/riverqueue/riverui) for inspecting and interacting with jobs and queues.
    
*   [Work functions](https://riverqueue.com/docs/work-functions) for simplified worker implementation.
    

\## Cross language enqueueing

River supports inserting jobs in some non-Go languages which are then worked by Go implementations. This may be desirable in performance sensitive cases so that jobs can take advantage of Go's fast runtime.

*   [Inserting jobs from Python](https://riverqueue.com/docs/python).
*   [Inserting jobs from Ruby](https://riverqueue.com/docs/ruby).

See [developing River](https://github.com/riverqueue/river/blob/master/docs/development.md).

Writing reliable workers
========================

One of the biggest benefits of River is that jobs can be [enqueued transactionally](/docs/transactional-enqueueing) and atomically along with other database changes. Once a job is committed to the database, River will not lose track of it and will ensure that it is executed.

However, even the most robust and reliable applications will inevitably encounter job errors or other failures, particularly at scale. Any River job may be retried multiple times due to scenarios including:

*   An error returned, raised, or thrown by the worker
*   An error preventing the completed job’s state from being saved to the database
*   A process crash or runtime failure

River is designed to [retry jobs](/docs/job-retries) in the event of an error. This at-least-once execution pattern ensures that programming errors, crashes, or transient network failures do not result in a job being lost or forgotten. It is therefore important to write workers with the expectation that jobs can and will be retried.

* * *

Jobs are automatically completed or errored[](#jobs-are-automatically-completed-or-errored)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

When River fetches a job, it passes the job to its registered worker. Successful completion marks the job completed asynchronously. A worker error records the failure and schedules a [retry](/docs/job-retries), or discards the job when its attempt budget is exhausted. Each language also has explicit outcomes for cancelling or snoozing.

* * *

Timeouts and cancellation[](#timeouts-and-contexts)
---------------------------------------------------

*   [Go](#tab-panel-0-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-0-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-0-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-0-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-0-4)

Go does not provide a way for a goroutine to cancel or terminate another goroutine. This means that the only practical way for River to timeout or cancel jobs is with [context](https://pkg.go.dev/context) cancellation.

Respect context cancellation

Workers should respect context cancellation for timeouts, job cancellation, and safe rapid shutdown. If a worker blocks and does not respect `ctx.Done()`, these features will not function and River will be stuck waiting for the job to complete.

To ensure that workers will always respect a cancelled or timed out context, **workers should always inherit from the context provided in `Work()`**.

Workers run on virtual threads. Check `context.checkCancelled()` between units of work and use interruptible I/O with timeouts. Java cannot forcibly terminate a handler that ignores interruption. See [graceful shutdown](/docs/graceful-shutdown).

River interrupts worker threads on timeout or cancellation. Let the exception propagate and put cleanup in `ensure` blocks. Avoid swallowing interruption exceptions or blocking indefinitely in native extensions, where interruption can be delayed.

Workers receive a cancellation token through `WorkContext`. Await it alongside long-running operations and return `WorkCancelled` when interrupted. Tokio can abort an asynchronous task that keeps yielding, but cannot reliably interrupt CPU-bound or blocking native code.

Workers receive an `AbortSignal`. Pass it to cancellable APIs and check it in loops. In-process JavaScript cannot forcibly stop a handler; CPU-bound handlers can use the optional worker-thread runtime. See [graceful shutdown](/docs/graceful-shutdown).

### Client job timeouts[](#client-job-timeouts)

The default job timeout is one minute. Disabling it also prevents ordinary timeout-based rescue of abandoned jobs, so do so only for jobs that need it.

*   [Go](#tab-panel-1-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-1-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-1-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-1-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-1-4)

By default, clients will time out all jobs after 1 minute (`DefaultJobTimeout`). This can be customized for all jobs at the client level with the `JobTimeout` config:

    client, err := river.NewClient(riverpgxv5.New(dbPool), &river.Config{    JobTimeout: 10*time.Minute,})

River can also run jobs with _no_ timeout, though it is not recommended to do this globally:

    client, err := river.NewClient(riverpgxv5.New(dbPool), &river.Config{    JobTimeout: -1,})

Set the attempt timeout on the client builder:

    builder.jobTimeout(Duration.ofMinutes(10));// Use a negative duration to disable timeouts.

Set `job_timeout` in seconds to change the client’s default time limit for an attempt:

    config = River::Config.new(job_timeout: 10 * 60)# Disable with job_timeout: nil.

Configure the default attempt timeout with `job_timeout` on the client builder:

    let client = riverqueue::Client::builder(pool)    .job_timeout(std::time::Duration::from_secs(10 * 60))    .build()?;// Use .without_job_timeout() to disable timeouts.

Set `jobTimeout` in the client configuration to change the default time limit for worker attempts:

    const client = new Client(driver, { jobTimeout: { minutes: 10 } });// Use jobTimeout: null to disable timeouts.

### Worker-level job timeouts[](#worker-level-job-timeouts)

*   [Go](#tab-panel-2-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-2-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-2-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-2-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-2-4)

Timeouts can also be customized at the level of an individual worker:

    func (w *MyWorker) Timeout(*Job[T]) time.Duration { return 30 * time.Second }

Some use cases require a job to run for an indefinite amount of time. To disable timeouts on a worker, return `-1`:

    func (w *MyWorker) Timeout(*Job[T]) time.Duration { return -1 }

Jobs with no timeout are still subject to being manually cancelled or an abrupt graceful shutdown via `StopAndCancel`, but this will only function if the worker respects the context’s cancellation.

Implement `Workers.Handler` and override `timeout` to set a limit for an individual worker. The callback receives the typed job, so it can also choose a duration based on its arguments:

    import com.riverqueue.Job;import com.riverqueue.WorkContext;import com.riverqueue.Workers;import java.time.Duration;
    builder.worker(myJob, new Workers.Handler<MyArgs>() {    @Override    public Duration timeout(Job<MyArgs> job) {        return Duration.ofSeconds(30);    }
        @Override    public void work(WorkContext<MyArgs> context) throws Exception {        performWork(context.args());    }});

Return `null` or `Duration.ZERO` to inherit `builder.jobTimeout`, as lambda handlers do. Return a negative duration such as `Duration.ofSeconds(-1)` to disable timeouts for this worker; cancellation and shutdown still apply.

River also calls `timeout` when evaluating abandoned jobs for rescue. Keep it safe for concurrent calls and free of side effects, and register compatible handlers on every client eligible to lead. Rescue respects longer worker deadlines and disabled timeouts.

Define `timeout` on the worker to override the client default for its attempts. The return value is a duration in seconds:

    def timeout(_job) = 30# Return nil to disable the timeout, or 0 to use the client default.

Override `timeout` in the worker’s trait implementation:

    fn timeout(&self, _job: &riverqueue::Job<MyArgs>) -> riverqueue::WorkerTimeout {    riverqueue::WorkerTimeout::After(std::time::Duration::from_secs(30))}// WorkerTimeout::Disabled disables the timeout for this kind.

Pass a `timeout` when registering the handler to give that worker its own attempt limit:

    workers.add(myJob, handler, { timeout: { seconds: 30 } });// Use timeout: null to disable it for this worker.

### Cancellation and shutdown[](#cancellation-and-shutdown)

A running job can be [cancelled remotely](/docs/cancelling-jobs) or interrupted during [shutdown](/docs/graceful-shutdown). Cooperate with the runtime’s cancellation mechanism and propagate interruption instead of reporting unfinished work as successful.

Job idempotency[](#job-idempotency)
-----------------------------------

A database’s [ACID properties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACID) will ensure that any particular insert operation occurs exactly once or errors. This guarantee can be augmented with [unique jobs](/docs/unique-jobs) so that only one job will be inserted based on a set of uniquely defining properties.

Once a job is inserted, it will be worked with _at least once_ semantics. A successful job in a normal system will run exactly once in the overwhelming majority number of cases, but there are exceptions. If the job errors, it’ll be reworked until it succeeds, and there may be side effects between these runs. Rarer cases are possible too, like if a job finishes successfully, but fails to be marked as completed, in which case it’ll be rescued and run again.

Jobs should be written so that they can still succeed even if run multiple times, which is generally accomplished by making every operation in the job idempotent.

### Idempotency with transactions[](#idempotency-with-transactions)

River workers have a shortcut to easier idempotency in that they can open a transaction in their work body, and in case of an error, roll changes back so that the next attempt will start with a clean slate.

*   [Go](#tab-panel-3-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-3-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-3-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-3-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-3-4)

Begin a transaction inside `Work` and defer rollback so early returns discard partial database changes. Commit only after the work succeeds:

    func (w *TxWorker) Work(ctx context.Context, job *river.Job[TxArgs]) error {    tx, err := w.dbPool.Begin(ctx)    if err != nil {        return err    }    defer tx.Rollback(ctx)
        ...
        if err != nil {        // Rollback occurs, reverting database changes made during the run.        return err    }
        return tx.Commit(ctx)}

Use `context.transaction` to commit application changes together or roll them back on failure:

    builder.worker(myJob, context -> {    context.transaction(connection -> {        performDatabaseWork(connection, context.job());        return null;    });});

Your database operations must still tolerate a repeated attempt. Use transactional completion below to commit the job’s completion alongside the changes.

Wrap the worker’s database operations in a Sequel transaction so they commit or roll back together:

    def work(job)  DB.transaction do    perform_database_work(job)  endend

Let errors escape the transaction so it rolls back.

Pass a transaction through the worker’s database operations and commit it only after they succeed:

    let mut tx = riverqueue::database::begin_postgres(&pool).await?;perform_database_work(&mut tx, &job).await?;tx.commit().await?;

Use one checked-out connection for the transaction. Roll back on failure and release the connection in `finally`:

    const tx = await pool.connect();
    try {  await tx.query("BEGIN");
      await performDatabaseWork(tx, job);
      await tx.query("COMMIT");} catch (error) {  await tx.query("ROLLBACK");  throw error;} finally {  tx.release();}

But it’s important to understand that **even a transaction is not a full idempotency guarantee**. Consider:

*   A work function may have called out to external systems while running like HTTP APIs or other non-transactional data stores (e.g. ElasticSearch). These changes will not roll back with a transaction.
    
*   To maximize work throughput, jobs are normally completed out-of-band of a work function, and in rare cases that completion could fail even if the worker succeeded and committed its transaction. See below for a possible remedy.
    

Transactions may also have performance and operational side effects. A long-lived transaction will tie up a Postgres backend while it’s open, and will contribute to database bloat as any rows still technically visible to the transaction have to be retained until it’s closed, even if they’ve since been deleted or updated to a new state. Workers may want to avoid opening a transaction when one isn’t needed, or when they’re expected to be long running.

### Transactionally completing jobs alongside other changes[](#transactionally-completing-jobs-alongside-other-changes)

*   [Go](#tab-panel-4-0)
*   [Java](#tab-panel-4-1)
*   [Ruby](#tab-panel-4-2)
*   [Rust](#tab-panel-4-3)
*   [TypeScript](#tab-panel-4-4)

A way to hedge against possible failures while completing a job and get a little closer to an _exactly once_ guarantee is to wrap operations in a transaction and complete the job as part of the same transaction using [`JobCompleteTx`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/riverqueue/river#JobCompleteTx). A successful commit guarantees that the job will never rerun. A failed commit discards all changes so the next run starts fresh.

    func (w *TxWorker) Work(ctx context.Context, job *river.Job[TxArgs]) error {    tx, err := w.dbPool.Begin(ctx)    if err != nil {        return err    }    defer tx.Rollback(ctx)
        ...
        _, err := river.JobCompleteTx[*riverpgxv5.Driver](ctx, tx, job)    if err != nil {        return err    }
        return tx.Commit(ctx)}

River normally completes jobs in large, efficient batches, so there is a throughput trade off to completing jobs in this way. Opening a transaction also has a small marginal cost, so that’ll add some overhead to the worker unless one was in use already.

See [transactional job completion](/docs/transactional-job-completion) for more details.

Call `context.complete(connection)` after your application writes, inside the same transaction. See [transactional job completion](/docs/transactional-job-completion) for the complete pattern.

Call `job.client.job_complete_tx(job)` after application writes inside the same transaction. Propagate errors so a rollback is retried. See [transactional job completion](/docs/transactional-job-completion) for the complete pattern.

Call `context.job_complete_tx(&mut tx).await?` after application writes and before committing the transaction. Propagate errors so a rollback is retried. See [transactional job completion](/docs/transactional-job-completion) for the complete pattern.

Call `await completeTx(tx)` from the worker context after application writes and before `COMMIT`. Propagate errors after a rollback. See [transactional job completion](/docs/transactional-job-completion) for the complete pattern.
